newsitem.title: CHINA: China treasury bond markets to prosper in 1997.
newsitem.headline: China treasury bond markets to prosper in 1997.

text.p: China's treasury bond markets are expected to grow in volume and importance in 1997 with T-bond spot and repurchase papers continuing to be the country's most active financial markets, analysts said on Thursday.

Beijing will continue to reform the issue and trading of T-bonds and bills, the hottest investment instruments of 1996, and falling inflation is expected to give an extra boost to the secondary market, they said.
But the experts declined to make a prediction about when T-bill futures might be revived.
T-bills were banned in 1995 after a series of huge trading scandals in Shanghai, which made Beijing lose patience with speculation in government debt futures.
Industry sources estimate that China will issue around 250 billion yuan ($30 billion) of debt next year, dramatically up on this year's total of 195.2 billion yuan, already an historical high.

Medium- and long-term T-bonds with maturities of three years and above are expected to account for most of the next year's issues in contrast with this year, when the bulk of Beijing's issuance consisted of short-term T-bills of one year or less, the sources said.

"There have been a lot of changes in the issuing of T-bonds this year, especially the introduction of a public tender system to set coupon rates," said Lu Weiming, a T-bond trader with China Guotai Securities.
"The reforms are expected to continue, pushing state debt returns closer to the markets' needs," he said.

Beijing this year opened the coupon rates to public tender by underwriters, bringing the rates much closer to market needs and making state debt more attractive to investors by abolishing a system in which administrative edict was used to decide T-bond returns.

"The share markets in Shanghai and Shenzhen are expected to stage a strong bull run next year with Beijing determined to support them in the run-up to Chinese takeover of Hong Kong," said a T-bond investment analyst.
"Liquidity will flow in and out of the stock markets in line with their erratic trading, which will make the T-bond repo and spot markets continue to be very active," he added.
The domestic share markets have surged this year with the official blessing of Beijing, enlivening the T-bond secondary markets, which have served as reservoirs of liquidity for the share markets.

In the first 10 months of this year, the combined volume of the T-bond repurchase and spot markets on the Shanghai stock exchange hit a record high of 1.3 trillion yuan, up 770 percent against the same 1995 period.
In comparison, trading of equity shares on the bourse totalled only 602 billion yuan, less than half the T-bond total.
"An expected cut in bank reserve ratios will be another important factor for the T-bond market next year," said Dai Yuzhong, a T-bond trader with J & A securities.

With inflation expected to fall to a year-on-year six percent this year against a year-on-year 14.8 percent last year, the People's Bank of China, the central bank, cut bank interest rates in May and August this year and has promised a cut in bank reserve ratios shortly.
Chinese banks and other financial institutions are required to place 13 percent of their deposits with the central bank and keep another five to seven percent for themselves as reserves.
Analysts said the ratio cut would release large amounts of money to the system and would help activate and buoy the T-bond markets.
